items.prompt: Per this unit's framework, what does an engineering level primarily measure?
choices: Raw technical skill — how hard a problem someone can solve once it's clearly defined
Scope — how much ambiguity someone resolves on their own, and how far the consequences and influence of their decisions extend
Years of tenure at the company
How many lines of code someone has shipped
items.explanation: Skill and scope are correlated but distinct — a highly skilled person kept on narrowly-scoped, well-defined tasks doesn't automatically read as operating at wide scope. Leveling conversations are fundamentally about scope: ambiguity tolerance, blast radius, time horizon, and influence radius.
items.reference:
Skill

Can you solve it once it's defined?

Scope

Do you decide what needs solving?

Why: the two are correlated but not the same axis — leveling measures scope, using skill only as one input to it.
items.learnMore:
Skill vs. scope

A capable engineer kept on narrowly-scoped tasks doesn't automatically read as senior. Someone still growing technically can be exactly the person who noticed and closed a cross-team gap nobody assigned them.

items.prompt: Why does this unit describe title as a "lagging indicator" rather than the definition of level?
choices: Because titles are assigned on a periodic cadence (review cycles) while actual scope expands continuously, so the two are expected to occasionally disagree
Because titles are entirely arbitrary and have no relationship to scope at all
Because only external hires have accurate titles
Because scope is defined by title, making the phrase circular
items.explanation: Scope typically expands continuously and unevenly across the four dimensions, while title changes happen at discrete moments (a promotion cycle). That mismatch is expected, not a sign the framework is broken — it's exactly why someone's actual scope and their current title can diverge in either direction.
items.reference:
📅 Titles change on a review cadence — quarterly, annually
📈 Actual scope expands continuously and unevenly

Why: a lagging indicator is expected to occasionally disagree with the thing it's tracking — that's not a sign the framework is broken.
items.learnMore:

↓

Someone can be operating wider than their title (the title hasn't caught up) or a title can have outrun current scope (a lateral hire, a retention bump). Neither means the framework failed.

Common mistake

Treating your current title as the ceiling of what you're allowed to attempt, instead of as a lagging report of what you've already been doing.

items.prompt: Which of the four scope dimensions asks "what breaks, and how widely, if your decision is wrong?"
choices: Ambiguity tolerance
Blast radius
Time horizon
Influence radius
items.explanation: Blast radius is specifically about the consequences of an incorrect decision — how far the damage would spread, not how undefined the problem was or how long the effects last.
items.reference:
❓ Ambiguity tolerance — how undefined can it be?
💥 Blast radius — what breaks if you're wrong?
⏳ Time horizon — this week's problem, or next year's?
🌐 Influence radius — your code, your team, or teams who've never met you?

Why: these four dimensions tend to expand together as level increases, but not always in lockstep.

items.prompt: Per L1, what question should you ask instead of "am I senior yet?"
choices: "How many years have I been at this company?"
"What's the largest, most ambiguous, most consequential piece of ambiguity I've resolved without being told exactly how?"
"How does my code quality compare to my peers?"
"When is the next promotion cycle?"
items.explanation: This reframed question points directly at scope — concrete, checkable evidence you can go collect — rather than at a label ("senior") that's assigned by someone else on a cadence you don't control.
items.reference:
❌ "Am I senior yet?" — asks about a label
✅ "What's the largest ambiguity I've resolved unasked?" — asks about scope

Why: the second question is what leveling conversations are actually trying to measure, not the org chart.
items.learnMore:
The practical reframe

Asking "am I senior yet" points at a label someone else assigns on a cadence you don't control. Asking "what's the largest, most ambiguous, most consequential thing I've resolved without being told exactly how" points at evidence you can go collect and act on this week.

Common mistake

Waiting for permission (a title, an explicit assignment) before attempting wider scope, instead of building the evidence trail that a title is supposed to lag behind.

items.explanation: The stages describe what's expected by default when ambiguity reaches someone, not a strict ladder where earlier-stage work disappears. Someone at the widest stage still does well-defined-task work — it's just no longer the thing that defines their role.

items.learnMore:
Stages, not a ladder you fully vacate

Someone operating at the "direction across teams" stage still writes code and still fixes well-defined tickets sometimes. The stage describes what's expected by default when ambiguity reaches them — at the earliest stage, someone else has already resolved the ambiguity before it arrives; at the latest, resolving ambiguity nobody assigned is the job.

Reading the four stages as a strict ladder where you stop doing the earlier-stage work entirely. It's additive, not a replacement.

items.prompt: Per L2, what produces the two most common sources of leveling friction?

items.explanation: L2 traces both common friction cases — someone's title lagging their actual scope, or a title that outran current scope — back to the same root cause: two different update cadences for a related but distinct pair of variables.

items.prompt: An engineer fixes the reported memory leak, notices the same pattern in three other files, fixes those too, and adds a lint rule so the pattern can't silently reappear — but does nothing beyond this service. Which response level is this?
choices: Response 1
Response 2 — project scope, bounded to this service
Response 3
Response 4
items.explanation: Fixing the pattern (not just the single instance) and adding a lint rule are both bounded to this one project/service — that's exactly Response 2's project scope, one step past the single reported symptom but not yet touching anything unowned or cross-team.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Fix the reported leak, ship it
2️⃣ + fix the pattern elsewhere, add a lint rule
3️⃣ + trend alerting, across adjacent services
4️⃣ + propose it as an org-wide platform default

Why: the technical fact and skill are identical at every level — what expands is the boundary of what's treated as "my problem."
items.learnMore:
Same fact, four boundaries

Response 1 fixes exactly the reported symptom. Response 2 generalizes to the pattern, still bounded to one project. Response 3 closes a gap nobody owned (no alerting at all). Response 4 turns the fix into a default the whole org inherits, requiring influence the person had to earn.

Common mistake

Assuming the higher-numbered response is always "more correct." Each is complete and correct for its own scope — the question is which scope actually matches the evidence in front of you.

items.prompt: In L3, Response 1 (fix exactly the reported leak, nothing more) is described as "complete, correct work." Why isn't this framed as a failure to operate at wider scope?
choices: It is a failure — every fix should always be expanded to the widest possible scope

items.explanation: Scope should track the evidence actually in front of you. Response 1 is complete for what was asked and what was visible at that point — expanding scope without evidence of a wider problem is scope creep, not seniority, per the first failure mode in L3.
items.reference:

❓ No evidence yet of a wider pattern to justify more

Treating every well-defined task as an opportunity that must be expanded, regardless of whether the evidence actually supports it.

items.prompt: Per L3's third failure mode, why might a well-reasoned proposal for an org-wide platform default get ignored if it comes from someone with no track record of shipping smaller-scoped work reliably?

items.explanation: L3 frames Response 4 as depending on trust built through Response 2/3-level delivery — influence radius doesn't expand just because someone attempts a wider-scope action; it expands because a track record makes others willing to extend that trust.

items.explanation: L3 explicitly cuts both ways: neither a single impressive incident nor a single narrowly-scoped (but correct) one should determine a leveling read by itself. The actual signal is a pattern across many situations over time.

Over-crediting or over-penalizing someone off one highly visible incident instead of asking whether it's representative.
